title: Support vector machines
summary: Separate labels coded as minus one and plus one by the widest slab that still respects every training point. Slack handles overlap; the width to compute is 2 over the length of w.
intuition:
A support vector machine looks for the boundary that stays as far as possible from the nearest training points. Labels are coded $-1$ and $+1$, so the predicted class is the sign of $w^\top x+b$. The two planes $w^\top x+b=\pm 1$ bound a slab. The distance between those planes, the geometric margin width, is $2/\|w\|$. Shortening $w$, once every point is forced to land on the correct side of its plane, is exactly widening that slab.

The points that sit on a margin plane have functional margin $1$. Those are the support vectors. A point with functional margin strictly above $1$ is outside the slab: deleting it does not change the same feasible $w$ and $b$. The fit is determined by the points on the boundary, not by a head-count of the whole sample.

If the two classes interleave, no single $w$ and $b$ can put every point on the correct side of the slab. The soft-margin objective keeps $\tfrac12\|w\|^2$ and adds $C$ times the total slack. Each slack $\xi_i\ge 0$ is the amount by which point $i$ is allowed to miss the margin constraint. Raising $C$ charges more for that total, so the optimum tolerates less slack. It does not add regularisation: the coefficient in front of $\|w\|^2$ stays $\tfrac12$, and a larger $C$ is the opposite of a larger ridge penalty. A kernel, if one is used at all, only swaps the ordinary dot product for another similarity; the margin geometry above is the part to compute.

definitions.body: For a point $(x_i,y_i)$ with $y_i\in\{-1,+1\}$, the functional margin is $y_i(w^\top x_i+b)$. The hard-margin constraints require it to be at least $1$.
The distance between the parallel planes $w^\top x+b=1$ and $w^\top x+b=-1$. It equals $2/\|w\|$. Each plane lies at distance $1/\|w\|$ from the decision boundary $w^\top x+b=0$.
In the hard-margin problem, a training point whose functional margin is exactly $1$. It lies on a margin plane. Points with functional margin greater than $1$ are not support vectors.

A slack $\xi_i\ge 0$ relaxes one constraint to $y_i(w^\top x_i+b)\ge 1-\xi_i$. The objective adds $C\sum_i\xi_i$. Larger $C$ penalises slack more heavily, which is less slack, not more regularisation.

formulas.name: Hard-margin primal
formulas.note: Labels are in $\{-1,+1\}$. Minimising $\|w\|$ maximises the geometric margin width $2/\|w\|$.

formulas.name: Geometric margin width
formulas.note: Distance between the planes $w^\top x+b=\pm 1$. The distance from the decision boundary to either plane is half of this, $1/\|w\|$.

formulas.name: Soft-margin primal
formulas.note: Larger $C$ weights the sum of slacks more. It is not a larger penalty on $\|w\|$.

properties: Scaling $(w,b)$ by a positive constant scales every functional margin by the same constant and leaves the decision boundary unchanged. The constraint $y_i(w^\top x_i+b)\ge 1$ fixes that scale, which is why the objective can just minimise $\|w\|$.
The geometric margin width is $2/\|w\|$. Halving $\|w\|$, if the constraints still hold, doubles the width.
Hard-margin support vectors are exactly the points with functional margin $1$. A feasible point with a larger functional margin can be removed without making that same $(w,b)$ infeasible.
The hard-margin problem is feasible only when the two classes are linearly separable. Overlapping classes need slack.

In the soft-margin objective the coefficient of $\|w\|^2$ is $\tfrac12$, independent of $C$. Raising $C$ punishes slack more, so the fit allows less of it. As $C$ grows, a separable dataset's soft-margin solution approaches the hard-margin solution.
A kernel replaces the dot product with a positive semidefinite similarity. It is an extension of this geometry, not a different margin formula.

examples.title: Two points on a line
examples.prompt: Labels are $-1$ at $x=-1$ and $+1$ at $x=3$. Find the hard-margin $w$ and $b$, and the geometric margin width $2/\|w\|$.
steps: Both points are support vectors, so both constraints are equalities: $(-1)(w\cdot(-1)+b)=1$ simplifies to $w-b=1$, and $(+1)(3w+b)=1$ simplifies to $3w+b=1$.
Adding the two equations gives $4w=2$, so $w=\tfrac12$. Then $\tfrac12-b=1$, so $b=-\tfrac12$. The second equation checks: $3\cdot\tfrac12-\tfrac12=1$.
The geometric margin width is $2/\|w\|=2/(\tfrac12)=4$. The decision boundary $\tfrac12 x-\tfrac12=0$ sits at $x=1$, halfway between $-1$ and $3$, and the points themselves are $4$ apart.
examples.answer: The solution is $w=\tfrac12$, $b=-\tfrac12$, and the geometric margin width is $4$.

examples.title: Three points, one of them not a support vector
examples.prompt: In the plane, $(2,2)$ and $(3,3)$ have label $+1$ and $(0,0)$ has label $-1$. Take $w=(\tfrac12,\tfrac12)$ and $b=-1$. Check the constraints, name the support vectors, and compute the geometric margin width.
steps: Functional margin of $(2,2)$: $(+1)(\tfrac12\cdot 2+\tfrac12\cdot 2-1)=1$. Functional margin of $(0,0)$: $(-1)(0+0-1)=1$. Both constraints are tight, so both points are support vectors.
Functional margin of $(3,3)$: $(+1)(\tfrac12\cdot 3+\tfrac12\cdot 3-1)=2$, which is strictly greater than $1$. The point is feasible and is not a support vector.

$\|w\|^2=\tfrac14+\tfrac14=\tfrac12$, so $\|w\|=\sqrt{1/2}$. The geometric margin width is $2/\|w\|=2\sqrt{2}$. That equals the distance from $(0,0)$ to $(2,2)$, because those two support vectors lie on the margin planes and the segment between them is parallel to $w$.
examples.answer: Support vectors are $(2,2)$ and $(0,0)$. The point $(3,3)$ has functional margin $2$ and is not a support vector. The geometric margin width is $2\sqrt{2}$.

traps: Calling $1/\|w\|$ the full geometric margin width. On this syllabus the geometric margin width is the distance between the two margin planes, $2/\|w\|$. The quantity $1/\|w\|$ is the distance from the decision boundary to one of those planes.
Treating a larger $C$ as a larger ridge penalty. $C$ multiplies the slacks. Raising it allows less slack. The term $\tfrac12\|w\|^2$ does not acquire a bigger coefficient.

Coding labels as $0$ and $1$ inside the constraint $y_i(w^\top x_i+b)\ge 1$. The algebra above needs $y_i\in\{-1,+1\}$. With a $0$ label the product $y_i(w^\top x_i+b)$ is identically $0$ and the constraint is impossible.
Declaring every training point a support vector. In the three-point example, $(3,3)$ has functional margin $2$ and does not define the slab.
Forcing a hard-margin fit on overlapping classes. If any point of each class sits in the convex hull of the other, the hard-margin constraints have no solution; slack is required.
python:
# 1-D hard margin: label -1 at x=-1, label +1 at x=3.
w = 0.5
b = -0.5
assert abs((w - b) - 1) < 1e-12
assert abs((3 * w + b) - 1) < 1e-12
width = 2 / abs(w)
assert abs(width - 4) < 1e-12
# 3-point check: functional margin of (3, 3) is 2; width squared is 8.
functional = 0.5 * 3 + 0.5 * 3 - 1
assert abs(functional - 2) < 1e-12
width_sq = (2 / (0.5 ** 2 + 0.5 ** 2) ** 0.5) ** 2
assert abs(width_sq - 8) < 1e-9
print(width)

questions.stem: A hard-margin SVM in one dimension has label $-1$ at $x=-2$ and label $+1$ at $x=2$. The geometric margin width $2/\|w\|$ is
questions.solution:
The answer is **A**, $4$.

Both constraints are tight: $(-1)(-2w+b)=1$ gives $2w-b=1$, and $2w+b=1$. Adding them yields $4w=2$, so $w=\tfrac12$ and $b=0$. The geometric margin width is $2/(\tfrac12)=4$, the distance between the two points. Option B is the distance from either point to the boundary at $0$.

questions.stem: In the soft-margin objective $\tfrac12\|w\|^2+C\sum_i\xi_i$, what does a larger value of $C$ mean?
options: Slack is penalised more heavily, so the fit tolerates less slack. This is not a stronger penalty on $\|w\|$.
It acts like a larger ridge penalty: $\|w\|$ is shrunk harder and the constraints are ignored.
Every slack is forced to equal $C$, whatever the points are.
The labels must be recoded from $\{-1,+1\}$ to $\{0,1\}$.
questions.solution:
The answer is **A**.

$C$ multiplies the sum of slacks only. The coefficient of $\|w\|^2$ remains $\tfrac12$. Raising $C$ makes each unit of slack more expensive, so the optimum uses less slack. That is the opposite of raising a ridge penalty, which is what B claims. $C$ is not itself a slack, and the label set does not change with $C$.

questions.stem: For the hard-margin solution $w=(\tfrac12,\tfrac12)$, $b=-1$ on the points $(2,2)$ with label $+1$, $(0,0)$ with label $-1$, and $(3,3)$ with label $+1$, which of the following are true?
options: $(2,2)$ and $(0,0)$ have functional margin $1$, so they are support vectors.
The point $(3,3)$ has functional margin $2$ and is not a support vector.
Every labelling of every finite point set has a feasible hard-margin solution.
questions.solution:
The correct options are **A, B, and C**.

The functional margins are $1$, $1$, and $2$ respectively, so only the first two points are support vectors. $\|w\|^2=\tfrac12$, hence $2/\|w\|=2\sqrt{2}$. D is false: if the classes are not linearly separable, the hard-margin inequalities have no solution.

questions.stem: Which of the following are true of the soft-margin primal on this syllabus?
options: A larger $C$ puts a heavier penalty on $\sum_i\xi_i$.
questions.solution:
The correct options are **A, B, and C**.

Slacks are nonnegative and each constraint gives way by exactly that slack. $C$ stands in front of the sum of slacks. The quadratic term keeps the coefficient $\tfrac12$ when $C$ changes, so D is the ridge-style misreading of $C$.

questions.stem: A hard-margin SVM uses label $-1$ at $x=-1$ and label $+1$ at $x=3$. Enter the geometric margin width $2/\|w\|$.
questions.solution:
The answer is **4**.

The active constraints are $w-b=1$ and $3w+b=1$. Adding them gives $4w=2$, so $w=\tfrac12$ and $b=-\tfrac12$. The geometric margin width is $2/(\tfrac12)=4$.
